# Drag and vortex-shedding frequency of surface-piercing circular cylinders towed at 5 × 10³ < Re < 5 × 10⁴

*FIRST DRAFT, 2026-10-30. Target: Experiments in Fluids (per notes.md).*

*Every number in this draft comes from `paper/make_paper_results.py`, which
reprocesses the raw files (see the "Notes for authors" section at the end). Items marked
**[TODO]** need information that is not in the project folder. Items marked **[CHECK]** are
decisions or values the authors must confirm before submission.*

**Authors:** [TODO]  **Affiliation:** [TODO]

## Abstract

We report the mean drag and in-line force fluctuations of smooth circular cylinders of
diameter D = 25.4, 38.1 and 50.8 mm towed through a water tank with a fixed
submerged length of 0.60 m. The Reynolds number spans 4.7 × 10³ ≤ Re ≤ 5.0 × 10⁴. Forces
were measured with a single-axis load cell calibrated in situ, and 29 tows were retained
for analysis. Over the full range, the mean drag coefficient is C_D = 1.15 ± 0.03
(mean ± standard deviation of individual runs). The three diameters agree within the
run-to-run scatter (mean C_D = 1.143, 1.152 and 1.157). The in-line force oscillates at twice the
vortex-shedding frequency. The corresponding Strouhal number is St = 0.200 ± 0.003,
independent of Re and D. Both results are consistent with classical subcritical-regime
data for circular cylinders. We also discuss the effects of blockage (2.3–4.5 %), the free
surface (Froude number Fr_D up to 2.2) and the cylinder's free end. **[CHECK: reframe once the
central claim of the paper is decided. See note A.]**

## 1 Introduction

Flow past a circular cylinder is the canonical bluff-body problem. In the subcritical regime
(roughly 10³ < Re < 2 × 10⁵), the boundary layer separates laminar and the drag coefficient
is nearly constant at C_D ≈ 1.0–1.2. Alternate vortex shedding occurs at a Strouhal
number St ≈ 0.2 (Roshko 1961; Achenbach 1968; Zdravkovich 1997; Norberg 2003)
**[CHECK all references]**. Because these values are well established, tow-tank measurements
in this range serve two purposes. They benchmark a facility and its force-measurement chain,
and they provide reference data for configurations that depart from the ideal
two-dimensional cylinder. Examples include finite immersion, a free surface and moderate blockage.

[TODO: 1–2 paragraphs motivating *this* study. Possible angles: (i) a characterised

at moderate Froude number (Chaplin & Teigen 2003 **[CHECK]**), (iii) a public benchmark
dataset. The current data support (i) and (iii) best. See note A.]

This paper describes the facility and the data-reduction procedure, including
temperature-corrected fluid properties and calibration, in §2. Mean drag and Strouhal number
for three diameters are presented in §3, and blockage, free-surface and end effects are
discussed in §4.

## 2 Experimental method

### 2.1 Facility and models

Experiments were conducted in a towing tank [TODO: name/institution] of width 0.90 m, water
depth 0.75 m and length [TODO]. The models were smooth circular cylinders of nominal diameter
1, 1.5 and 2 in (D = 25.4, 38.1 and 50.8 mm) [TODO: material, surface finish, measured
diameter]. Each cylinder was mounted vertically from the carriage, pierced the free surface,
and had a submerged length L = 0.60 m **[CHECK, see note B]**. This leaves a gap of
0.15 m between the free end and the tank floor [TODO: end condition, e.g. open or capped].
The aspect ratios L/D are 23.6, 15.7 and 11.8. The geometric blockage ratio
β = DL/(WH) is 2.3, 3.4 and 4.5 % respectively (Table 1).

The carriage towed each model at nominal speeds U = 0.2–1.1 m/s in 0.1 m/s steps
[TODO: carriage drive, how speed was set and verified, speed uncertainty, rest time
between runs]. Water temperature was logged for every run. It was 16.9–17.6 °C (D = 25.4 mm,
14 Oct 2025), 15.0–15.6 °C (D = 50.8 mm, 3 Nov 2025) and 13.7–14.3 °C (D = 38.1 mm,
12 Mar 2026).

### 2.2 Force measurement and calibration

Drag was measured with a single-axis load cell [TODO: model, range, how it was mounted, and
whether the measured force includes any part of the mount above the waterline]. The cell
was sampled at 200 Hz. It was calibrated in situ with dead weights of 0–2 kg, loaded and then
unloaded, before each test campaign. A linear fit gives a sensitivity of
0.020006 ± 0.000009 V/N (September 2025, used for the 25.4 and 50.8 mm cylinders) and
0.021292 ± 0.000014 V/N (March 2026, after the load cell was remounted, used for the
38.1 mm cylinder). Standard errors are from the fit. The largest calibration residual,
including loading/unloading hysteresis, is 0.016–0.017 N in both cases.

### 2.3 Data reduction

Each record is 12 s long (Fig. 1a). The zero is the mean output over 0 < t < 1 s, before the
carriage moves. The carriage reaches steady speed at t ≈ 2.5 s and decelerates at
t ≈ 9 s in every run. The mean drag F_D and the RMS fluctuation F′ are computed over the
window 3 < t < 8 s. The window was fixed in time for all runs, so it covers between
20D (D = 50.8 mm, U = 0.2 m/s) and 217D (D = 25.4 mm, U = 1.1 m/s) of travel. The means of
the first and second halves of the window differ by less than 0.5 % in every retained run,
which indicates that start-up transients have decayed.

The drag coefficient and Reynolds number are

  C_D = F_D / (½ ρ U² D L),  Re = U D / ν,

with ρ(T) from Tanaka et al. (2001) and μ(T) from the Vogel equation, both evaluated at the
logged water temperature of each run **[CHECK: cite a standard source for μ(T)]**.
Using the 20 °C value ν = 1.004 × 10⁻⁶ m²/s would overestimate Re by 6–17 %. It would change
C_D by less than 0.1 % through ρ.

The shedding frequency is obtained from the peak of the Hann-windowed periodogram of the
in-line force over the same window (Fig. 1b). For a cylinder the in-line force fluctuates at
twice the shedding frequency, so f_s = f_peak/2 and St = f_s D/U. The 5 s window limits the
frequency resolution to 0.2 Hz. This gives a St resolution of about ±6 % at the lowest
f_peak (D = 50.8 mm, U = 0.2 m/s) and below ±1 % at the highest speeds.

### 2.4 Data quality and exclusions

Run 17 (D = 50.8 mm, U = 0.8 m/s) was excluded. In that run the load-cell output drifted
monotonically during the tow, and the post-tow zero was offset by 4.2 N (Fig. 2, open
symbol). In all other runs the post-tow zero returned to within 0.004 N of the pre-tow zero.
The run log notes a small residual wave from the preceding tow in run 4. That run shows no
anomaly and is retained.

## 3 Results

### 3.1 Force signals

Figure 1(a) shows a typical record (D = 25.4 mm, U = 0.6 m/s). The force rises over
≈ 0.7 s as the carriage accelerates, then holds a steady mean with a regular oscillation. The
spectrum (Fig. 1b) has a single sharp peak at 9.4 Hz, 2–3 decades above the background,
which corresponds to f_s = 4.7 Hz. The RMS in-line force coefficient C_D′ = F′/(½ρU²DL)
is 0.05–0.07 in all runs. It is largest at the lowest speeds, where the
calibration residual is a larger fraction of the signal.

![Figure 1](fig1_trace_spectrum.png)

**Figure 1.** (a) In-line force for D = 25.4 mm, U = 0.6 m/s (run 5). The shaded region is
the averaging window. (b) Normalised power spectral density of the force in the averaging
window.

### 3.2 Drag coefficient

Figure 2 shows C_D versus Re for all retained runs, and Table 2 summarises the results. All
29 values lie between 1.09 and 1.22. The diameter-averaged values are 1.143 ± 0.010,
1.152 ± 0.008 and 1.157 ± 0.011 (mean ± standard error) for D = 25.4, 38.1 and 50.8 mm. The
largest difference, 0.014 between the 50.8 and 25.4 mm cylinders, is not statistically
significant (Welch t = 0.9). The pooled mean is C_D = 1.151 ± 0.030 (s.d.).

For the 25.4 and 38.1 mm cylinders, C_D increases weakly with Re, by 0.11 and 0.07 per decade
respectively. The 50.8 mm cylinder shows no trend (−0.01 per decade). Because each cylinder
covers a different Re range at the same set of speeds, Re and Fr_D vary together within each
series. The present data therefore cannot attribute this weak trend to Re, Fr_D, or a
speed-dependent systematic error (§4.2).

![Figure 2](fig2_cd_vs_re.png)

**Figure 2.** Drag coefficient versus Reynolds number. The open triangle is run 17, which was
excluded because of load-cell zero drift (§2.4). No blockage correction is applied.

**Table 2.** Summary by diameter (excluding run 17). Uncertainties are standard deviation
(s.d.) or standard error (s.e.) over runs.

| D (mm) | n | C_D (mean) | s.d. | s.e. | C_D′ (mean) | St (mean ± s.d.) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 25.4 | 10 | 1.143 | 0.033 | 0.010 | 0.056 | 0.200 ± 0.002 |
| 38.1 | 10 | 1.152 | 0.026 | 0.008 | 0.055 | 0.199 ± 0.004 |
| 50.8 | 9 | 1.157 | 0.034 | 0.011 | 0.054 | 0.202 ± 0.003 |
| all | 29 | 1.151 | 0.030 | 0.006 | 0.055 | 0.200 ± 0.003 |

### 3.3 Strouhal number

The Strouhal number (Fig. 3) is 0.200 ± 0.003 over all runs, with no dependence on Re or D
beyond the frequency-resolution limit described in §2.3. The lowest value, 0.191 (D = 38.1 mm,
U = 0.2 m/s), is within one resolution step of 0.20. This agrees with the accepted
subcritical value St ≈ 0.20–0.21 (Norberg 2003 **[CHECK]**).

![Figure 3](fig3_strouhal.png)

**Figure 3.** Strouhal number from the in-line force spectrum (St = f_peak D / 2U). The
dashed line is St = 0.2.

## 4 Discussion

### 4.1 Comparison with two-dimensional data

[TODO: overlay or tabulate reference C_D(Re) data, e.g. Wieselsberger (1922) and Roshko
(1961), on Fig. 2.] For two-dimensional cylinders in the range 5 × 10³ < Re < 5 × 10⁴,
C_D is typically 1.0–1.2 **[CHECK against the specific sources cited]**. The present
uncorrected mean of 1.15 lies within this range. The Strouhal number matches 2D values
closely.

### 4.2 Blockage, free-surface and end effects

*Blockage.* The geometric blockage ratio is 2.3–4.5 %. Blockage increases the measured
drag, so the corrected C_D would be lower and the correction largest for the 50.8 mm
cylinder. Applying a standard correction (e.g. Allen & Vincenti 1944; Maskell 1963; West &
Apelt 1982) is **[TODO / CHECK: choose the method and report corrected values]**. Any
correction proportional to β would reduce the small, non-significant increase of C_D with D
in Table 2.

*Free surface.* The cylinders pierce the free surface. The diameter Froude number
Fr_D = U/√(gD) reaches 2.2 for the 25.4 mm cylinder, high enough for a bow wave and
ventilated wake to form near the surface [TODO: observations or photos?]. The added
pressure drag near the surface depends on Fr_D. This could cause the weak increase in C_D
with speed for the smaller cylinders, but the present data cannot separate it from
Re. A test at fixed Re and varying Fr_D (e.g. different water temperatures or
immersion depths) would distinguish the two.

*Free end.* The cylinders end 0.15 m above the tank floor. Flow around a free end lowers the
local sectional drag over a few diameters (Zdravkovich 1997 **[CHECK]**). For L/D = 12–24 this
effect would bias the total C_D low relative to 2D values, partly offsetting blockage.

### 4.3 Limitations

Each condition was towed once. The three diameters were tested on different dates, with
different water temperatures and, for D = 38.1 mm, after the load cell was remounted and
recalibrated. Diameter is therefore confounded with test campaign. That the three
campaigns agree within 1.3 % is itself evidence of good reproducibility. Repeat tows and
at least one diameter repeated across campaigns would strengthen the paper considerably.

## 5 Conclusions

def water_rho(T):
    # Tanaka et al. (2001), kg/m^3
    a1, a2, a3, a4, a5 = -3.983035, 301.797, 522528.9, 69.34881, 999.974950
    return a5 * (1 - (T + a1) ** 2 * (T + a2) / (a3 * (T + a4)))


def water_mu(T):
    # Vogel equation, Pa s
    return 2.414e-5 * 10 ** (247.8 / (T + 273.15 - 140.0))


def sensitivity(path):
    cal = pd.read_csv(path)
    p, cov = np.polyfit(cal.mass_g / 1000 * G, cal.voltage_V, 1, cov=True)

## Abstract

We report the mean drag and in-line force fluctuations of smooth circular cylinders of
diameter D = 25.4, 38.1 and 50.8 mm towed through a water tank with a fixed
submerged length of 0.60 m. The Reynolds number spans 4.7 × 10³ ≤ Re ≤ 5.0 × 10⁴. Forces

run-to-run scatter (mean C_D = 1.143, 1.152 and 1.157). The in-line force oscillates at twice the

independent of Re and D. Both results are consistent with classical subcritical-regime

Flow past a circular cylinder is the canonical bluff-body problem. In the subcritical regime
(roughly 10³ < Re < 2 × 10⁵), the boundary layer separates laminar and the drag coefficient
is nearly constant at C_D ≈ 1.0–1.2. Alternate vortex shedding occurs at a Strouhal

and they provide reference data for configurations that depart from the ideal
two-dimensional cylinder. Examples include finite immersion, a free surface and moderate blockage.

## Abstract

We report the mean drag and in-line force fluctuations of smooth circular cylinders of
diameter D = 25.4, 38.1 and 50.8 mm towed through a water tank with a fixed
submerged length of 0.60 m. The Reynolds number spans 4.7 × 10³ ≤ Re ≤ 5.0 × 10⁴. Forces
were measured with a single-axis load cell calibrated in situ, and 29 tows were retained
for analysis. Over the full range, the mean drag coefficient is C_D = 1.15 ± 0.03
(mean ± standard deviation of individual runs). The three diameters agree within the
run-to-run scatter (mean C_D = 1.143, 1.152 and 1.157). The in-line force oscillates at twice the
vortex-shedding frequency. The corresponding Strouhal number is St = 0.200 ± 0.003,
independent of Re and D. Both results are consistent with classical subcritical-regime
data for circular cylinders. We also discuss the effects of blockage (2.3–4.5 %), the free
surface (Froude number Fr_D up to 2.2) and the cylinder's free end. **[CHECK: reframe once the
central claim of the paper is decided. See note A.]**

## 1 Introduction

Flow past a circular cylinder is the canonical bluff-body problem. In the subcritical regime
(roughly 10³ < Re < 2 × 10⁵), the boundary layer separates laminar and the drag coefficient
is nearly constant at C_D ≈ 1.0–1.2. Alternate vortex shedding occurs at a Strouhal
number St ≈ 0.2 (Roshko 1961; Achenbach 1968; Zdravkovich 1997; Norberg 2003)
**[CHECK all references]**. Because these values are well established, tow-tank measurements
in this range serve two purposes. They benchmark a facility and its force-measurement chain,
and they provide reference data for configurations that depart from the ideal
two-dimensional cylinder. Examples include finite immersion, a free surface and moderate blockage.

[TODO: 1–2 paragraphs motivating *this* study. Possible angles: (i) a characterised

1, 1.5 and 2 in (D = 25.4, 38.1 and 50.8 mm) [TODO: material, surface finish, measured

The carriage towed each model at nominal speeds U = 0.2–1.1 m/s in 0.1 m/s steps
[TODO: carriage drive, how speed was set and verified, speed uncertainty, rest time

Drag was measured with a single-axis load cell [TODO: model, range, how it was mounted, and

Run 17 (D = 50.8 mm, U = 0.8 m/s) was excluded. In that run the load-cell output drifted

## 3 Results

### 3.1 Force signals

Figure 1(a) shows a typical record (D = 25.4 mm, U = 0.6 m/s). The force rises over
≈ 0.7 s as the carriage accelerates, then holds a steady mean with a regular oscillation. The
spectrum (Fig. 1b) has a single sharp peak at 9.4 Hz, 2–3 decades above the background,
which corresponds to f_s = 4.7 Hz. The RMS in-line force coefficient C_D′ = F′/(½ρU²DL)
is 0.05–0.07 in all runs. It is largest at the lowest speeds, where the
calibration residual is a larger fraction of the signal.

![Figure 1](fig1_trace_spectrum.png)

**Figure 1.** (a) In-line force for D = 25.4 mm, U = 0.6 m/s (run 5). The shaded region is
the averaging window. (b) Normalised power spectral density of the force in the averaging
window.

### 3.2 Drag coefficient

Figure 2 shows C_D versus Re for all retained runs, and Table 2 summarises the results. All
29 values lie between 1.09 and 1.22. The diameter-averaged values are 1.143 ± 0.010,
1.152 ± 0.008 and 1.157 ± 0.011 (mean ± standard error) for D = 25.4, 38.1 and 50.8 mm. The
largest difference, 0.014 between the 50.8 and 25.4 mm cylinders, is not statistically
significant (Welch t = 0.9). The pooled mean is C_D = 1.151 ± 0.030 (s.d.).

For the 25.4 and 38.1 mm cylinders, C_D increases weakly with Re, by 0.11 and 0.07 per decade
respectively. The 50.8 mm cylinder shows no trend (−0.01 per decade). Because each cylinder
covers a different Re range at the same set of speeds, Re and Fr_D vary together within each
series. The present data therefore cannot attribute this weak trend to Re, Fr_D, or a
speed-dependent systematic error (§4.2).

### 3.3 Strouhal number

The Strouhal number (Fig. 3) is 0.200 ± 0.003 over all runs, with no dependence on Re or D
beyond the frequency-resolution limit described in §2.3. The lowest value, 0.191 (D = 38.1 mm,
U = 0.2 m/s), is within one resolution step of 0.20. This agrees with the accepted
subcritical value St ≈ 0.20–0.21 (Norberg 2003 **[CHECK]**).

![Figure 3](fig3_strouhal.png)

**Figure 3.** Strouhal number from the in-line force spectrum (St = f_peak D / 2U). The
dashed line is St = 0.2.

## 4 Discussion

### 4.1 Comparison with two-dimensional data

[TODO: overlay or tabulate reference C_D(Re) data, e.g. Wieselsberger (1922) and Roshko
(1961), on Fig. 2.] For two-dimensional cylinders in the range 5 × 10³ < Re < 5 × 10⁴,
C_D is typically 1.0–1.2 **[CHECK against the specific sources cited]**. The present
uncorrected mean of 1.15 lies within this range. The Strouhal number matches 2D values
closely.

### 4.2 Blockage, free-surface and end effects

*Blockage.* The geometric blockage ratio is 2.3–4.5 %. Blockage increases the measured
drag, so the corrected C_D would be lower and the correction largest for the 50.8 mm
cylinder. Applying a standard correction (e.g. Allen & Vincenti 1944; Maskell 1963; West &
Apelt 1982) is **[TODO / CHECK: choose the method and report corrected values]**. Any
correction proportional to β would reduce the small, non-significant increase of C_D with D
in Table 2.

*Free surface.* The cylinders pierce the free surface. The diameter Froude number
Fr_D = U/√(gD) reaches 2.2 for the 25.4 mm cylinder, high enough for a bow wave and
ventilated wake to form near the surface [TODO: observations or photos?]. The added
pressure drag near the surface depends on Fr_D. This could cause the weak increase in C_D
with speed for the smaller cylinders, but the present data cannot separate it from
Re. A test at fixed Re and varying Fr_D (e.g. different water temperatures or
immersion depths) would distinguish the two.

*Free end.* The cylinders end 0.15 m above the tank floor. Flow around a free end lowers the
local sectional drag over a few diameters (Zdravkovich 1997 **[CHECK]**). For L/D = 12–24 this
effect would bias the total C_D low relative to 2D values, partly offsetting blockage.

### 4.3 Limitations

Each condition was towed once. The three diameters were tested on different dates, with
different water temperatures and, for D = 38.1 mm, after the load cell was remounted and
recalibrated. Diameter is therefore confounded with test campaign. That the three
campaigns agree within 1.3 % is itself evidence of good reproducibility. Repeat tows and
at least one diameter repeated across campaigns would strengthen the paper considerably.

## 5 Conclusions

The current draft (`paper/draft.md`) already deals with all three reviewer comments. The reviewers seem to have read an older version, probably the `analysis.ipynb` numbers, which used 20 °C fluid properties and kept run 17. I made one small addition and changed nothing else.

I checked the draft's numbers with my own script, which reads the raw files, calibration files and run log directly. Every Re and C_D matches `paper/run_table.csv`. I couldn't re-run `make_paper_results.py` itself because numpy, pandas and matplotlib aren't installed here, so the figures were not regenerated (they don't need to change).

**Reviewer 1.1 (Re at the measured temperature):** Already done. §2.3 says ρ and ν are evaluated at each run's logged temperature (13.7–17.6 °C). Using 20 °C would overstate Re by 6.0–17.2 %, which matches the draft's "6–17 %". The temperature ranges in §2.1 and Table 1 match the log.

**Reviewer 1.2 (run 17):** Already excluded, and §2.4 says so. The data back this up:
- After the tow, run 17's zero is off by +4.20 N. In every other run it comes back within 0.0034 N.
- Its force keeps rising through the averaging window (12.4 → 14.4 N). The neighbouring runs stay flat to within 0.1 %.
- Its C_D would be 1.355. Including it raises the 50.8 mm mean from 1.157 to 1.177.

**My edit:** The reviewer asked whether the run was corrected or excluded. I added a sentence to §2.4 explaining why it wasn't corrected: the drift built up during the tow rather than as a step offset, so re-zeroing can't remove it.

**Reviewer 2.1 (Re range in abstract):** Already there: "4.7 × 10³ ≤ Re ≤ 5.0 × 10⁴" (the data give 4 690 to 49 912).

**Draft response to reviewers:**
> **R1.1** We agree. ρ and ν are now evaluated at the measured water temperature of each run (13.7–17.6 °C), using Tanaka et al. (2001) and the Vogel equation (§2.3, Table 1). Using 20 °C properties overstated Re by 6–17 % and changed C_D by less than 0.1 %.
> **R1.2** Run 17 has been excluded (§2.4). Its post-tow zero was offset by 4.2 N, against below 0.004 N in every other run. Its output also rose steadily during the tow. A drift of that kind can't be removed by re-zeroing, so we did not try to correct the run. It is shown as an open symbol in Fig. 2. Without it, the apparent rise of C_D with diameter goes away (C_D = 1.143, 1.152 and 1.157).
> **R2.1** The abstract now states the range: 4.7 × 10³ ≤ Re ≤ 5.0 × 10⁴.

**Before you resubmit:**
- **Title:** It says "5 × 10³ < Re < 5 × 10⁴", but the lowest Re is 4 690, so it contradicts the abstract. I left it alone. Something like "Re ≈ 5 × 10³–5 × 10⁴" would fix it.
- **Open author notes:** The draft's notes A, B and D are still unresolved. Note B is the most important: the submerged length L was changed from 0.70 to 0.60 m after the first C_D "looked low", and nothing in the folder records how L was measured. A reviewer could easily ask about it next.
